category: kabbalistic treatise (on the reasons for the commandments)

date.note: Composed in 1287 in Castile, on the dating accepted in the scholarship (Scholem; Wolfson's critical edition). It is one of the Hebrew works Moses de Leon wrote under his own name in the years around 1290.

summary: Sefer ha-Rimmon ('the Book of the Pomegranate'), composed by the Castilian kabbalist Moses de Leon in 1287, is a Hebrew treatise on the mystical reasons and inner meanings of the commandments (ta'amei ha-mitzvot). It is one of the works de Leon wrote under his own name, distinct from the Zohar that modern scholarship attributes to him, and it develops a kabbalistic theory of the commandments in relation to the sefirot. It was critically edited by Elliot R. Wolfson (Brown Judaic Studies, 1988).
description:
Sefer ha-Rimmon (the 'Book of the Pomegranate') is a Hebrew kabbalistic treatise composed by Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon (c. 1240-1305) in Castile in 1287. It belongs to the group of works that de Leon wrote and circulated under his own name, and it is therefore, unlike the Zohar (which he circulated as the ancient teaching of the second-century Shimon bar Yochai and which modern scholarship attributes to him), a work whose authorship is not in dispute.

The treatise is devoted to the reasons and inner meanings of the commandments, the ta'amei ha-mitzvot: it interprets the observances of Jewish law in mystical and kabbalistic terms, relating their performance to the dynamics of the divine potencies, the ten sefirot, and to the effect of human action upon the supernal world. In doing so it gives expression to the theosophy of the hidden Ein Sof and the emanated sefirot that is the heart of the Kabbalah taking shape in thirteenth-century Castile, the same body of ideas that the Zohar develops. In the modern scholarship the book is valued both in its own right, as a systematic kabbalistic account of the commandments, and for the light it throws on the Zohar: because de Leon's signed Hebrew works and the Zohar share terminology, imagery, and doctrine, the signed works have been central to the argument, made in detail by Gershom Scholem, that de Leon composed the bulk of the Zohar, and they remain a principal comparative witness in the study of the Zohar's language and formation.

Sefer ha-Rimmon survives and has been critically edited: Elliot R. Wolfson's edition, The Book of the Pomegranate: Moses de Leon's Sefer ha-Rimmon (Brown Judaic Studies, 1988), establishes the Hebrew text with an introductory study and is available in open access through the Brown Judaic Studies repository. This entry presents the work on the tradition's own terms as a kabbalistic treatise on the reasons for the commandments and records the scholarly account of its authorship, its date, and its relation to the Zohar; the scholarly attribution of the Zohar to de Leon, to which the book is relevant, is recorded as the academic position within the wider, unadjudicated dispute over the Zohar's authorship, exactly as in the moses-de-leon and zohar entries.
